# How the proof works: Kourovka 21.38

**Agent-generated exposition; not refereed.** This informal account was generated by **Nilradical v0** after human acceptance of the linked proof snapshot. It has not undergone human review or refereeing and may simplify details. The exact mathematical claims are the linked Lean statements and their proofs; human acceptance of that snapshot does not imply human review of this exposition. The [human decision](../nilradical-v0-acceptance/README.md) and [technical verification](../nilradical-v0-verification/README.md) are separate records.

The answer is an explicit infinite group of ordinary spread exactly one. Every nonidentity element has a companion with which it generates the whole group, but two particular nonidentity elements have no common companion. This answers both Donoven and Harper's original infinite-group question and the unrestricted existence question recorded as Kourovka 21.38. The [public statement](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_38/Statement.lean#L14) keeps these formulations separate as `OriginalQuestion` and `NotebookStatement`.

Ordinary generation matters here. `GeneratesPair x y` means that the subgroup generated by the two elements is the entire group. For a natural number $k$, `HasSpreadAtLeast G k` asks for a common generating companion for every $k$-tuple of nonidentity elements; repetitions are permitted. The final theorem `diagonal_spread_profile` proves that this property holds exactly when $k \le 1$. Thus “exactly one” agrees with the maximum convention for spread, including its behavior on longer tuples. These definitions impose no conjugacy restriction on the companion.

The witness comes from Thompson's group $F$, represented concretely as increasing permutations of the rationals. They fix everything outside the open unit interval and are affine on a finite dyadic subdivision inside it, with slopes that are integer powers of two. This rational model is enough for the abstract existence question. Its elements are actual maps, and the relevant generation and fixed-point properties are proved about those maps.

Near zero, an element $f$ has the form $f(t) = 2^m t$; near one, it has the form $f(t) = 1 + 2^n(t-1)$, for unique integers $m$ and $n$. Composition adds these exponents. The [endpoint construction](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_38/Proof/EndpointSlopes.lean#L163) packages them into `endpointCharacter`. Its subgroup `diagonalSubgroup` consists of maps with $m = n$. In familiar notation, if $\pi(f) = (m,n)$, the witness is $G = \pi^{-1}(\mathbb{Z}(1,1))$. Existence and uniqueness of the affine germs justify this description without introducing derivatives as unexplained data.

The proof's two halves exploit the same endpoint equality differently. To generate $G$, it suffices to obtain all maps trivial near the endpoints and one map whose endpoint exponents are $(1,1)$. To obstruct a common companion, equal slopes force each element to have an interior fixed point. The first assertion requires substantial local generation theory; the second gives a short action argument.

Write $F^{\prime}$ for the compact core, consisting of maps that are the identity in neighborhoods of both endpoints. The formalization identifies it with the endpoint kernel and with the derived subgroup, then proves that it is perfect: every core element is a product of commutators of core elements. The precise algebraic bridge is `compactCore_commutator_eq` in [the core argument](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_38/Proof/CorePerfect.lean#L37). Perfectness is what later converts local agreement of maps into containment of an entire subgroup.

Now fix any $f \ne 1$ in $G$. The companion construction specializes **Gili Golan-Polak's published prescribed-generation theorem**, Proposition 16(1) of [*Thompson's group F is almost 3/2-generated*](https://doi.org/10.1112/blms.12841), to endpoint exponents $(1,1)$. This is a formal proof of the required case of that known theorem, not a claim that Nilradical v0 discovered the theorem. The local generation mechanism also follows Golan's [*The generation problem in Thompson group F*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.02572v2), especially its interval-motion and interpolation arguments.

Binary words describe dyadic intervals, and paired words describe affine branches between them. Starting from movement by $f$ or its inverse, the construction produces a finite tree-pair map $g$. Its branches connect sufficiently deep descendants of interior intervals. It also supplies a one-sided slope change beside an interval on which $g$ is the identity. The proposition `GenerationData f g` records these proved facts, including a nontrivial core element in $H = \langle f,g\rangle$. Crucially, `exists_generationData` requires only $f \ne 1$. The argument therefore includes $f$ in $F^{\prime}$, where both endpoint exponents vanish.

The next task is to assemble branch information into genuine elements of $H$. For any core map and any compact interior interval, the proof constructs an element of $H \cap F^{\prime}$ agreeing with that map throughout the interval. Conjugated powers of the one-sided slope witness correct successive branches while preserving earlier agreement. A finite refinement makes the corrections compatible, and an additional adjustment cancels the endpoint characters. The result is exact agreement by one subgroup element on the entire chosen interval.

Interval motion needs care because the action is on rational points. A bounded rational orbit can have an irrational supremum. The proof therefore excludes invariant interior **real cuts** for the relevant interval fixers, which justifies the compression used in interpolation. Merely knowing that there is no common rational fixed point would not supply this step. [`GenerationData.coreLocalInterpolation`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_38/Proof/PrescribedGeneration.lean#L20) gathers the motion, refinement, and correction results into the needed interpolation theorem.

Two carefully chosen interpolations then recover each commutator of core maps as a commutator of elements already in $H$. Supports control the equality: the first replacement agrees on the support needed by the second map, and the second replacement agrees on the support needed by the first replacement. Perfectness gives $F^{\prime} \le H$. For any $z$ in $G$, write $\pi(z) = (n,n)$. Since $\pi(g) = (1,1)$, the element $zg^{-n}$ lies in $F^{\prime}$ and hence in $H$. Therefore $z$ lies in $H$. This final kernel-and-quotient argument is [proved explicitly](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_38/Proof/DiagonalGeneration.lean#L29), and `exists_generating_companion` discharges every hypothesis for the constructed pair.

For the upper bound, an element $y$ in $G$ has equal endpoint slopes $s$. If $s \ne 1$, the displacement $y(t)-t$ has opposite signs near the two endpoints. If $s = 1$, an endpoint neighborhood is already fixed. In the first case, a finite affine subdivision locates a sign crossing, and solving the corresponding affine equation gives a **rational** interior fixed point. Thus the obstruction occurs in the actual rational action. This specializes the fixed-point obstruction in Golan-Polak's [*The spread of Thompson's group F*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.19444v1), Lemma 2 and Remark 11.

Choose two nonidentity core maps $a$ and $b$ with disjoint interior supports. Every interior point is fixed by at least one of them. Given any proposed common companion $y$, take its interior fixed point $z$. Then either $\langle a,y\rangle$ or $\langle b,y\rangle$ fixes $z$. The full group $G$ moves every interior point, so that stabilizer is proper and the relevant pair cannot generate $G$. [`diagonal_exists_pair_no_common_companion`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_38/Proof/UpperBound.lean#L105) formalizes this order of quantifiers: the obstructing pair is fixed before the companion is chosen. Infinitude is proved separately by distinct powers of an increasing core map that moves a point.
